entities.name: Epic of King Gesar
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Epic of King Gesar is a monumental epic poem originating in East Asia, specifically among the Tibetan and Mongolian cultures, with roots tracing back over a millennium, likely solidified in written form during the 11th century CE. This work is not merely a literary treasure; it embodies the spiritual and cultural ethos of the Tibetan people, showcasing the heroism of King Gesar, who is depicted as a divinely chosen figure destined to protect his people against various evils. The epic serves as a crucial artifact linking mythology, oral tradition, and historical events, acting as a conduit for understanding the social and spiritual dynamics of the Tibetan plateau and surrounding regions.

The narrative follows King Gesar's heroic exploits, depicting battles against demons and tyrants, his journeys across vast landscapes, and his complex relationships with both allies and adversaries. These stories were transmitted orally for generations before being recorded, reflecting not only the valor of Gesar but also the values and aspirations of the societies that revered him. The epic is noted for its rich imagery and profound philosophical insights, making it a pivotal text in Tibetan Buddhism and influencing regional folklore.

The legacy of the Epic of King Gesar is profound, as it has inspired countless adaptations in literature, theater, and even modern media, serving as a bedrock for Tibetan cultural identity. Its themes of heroism and moral integrity resonate beyond its geographic origins, influencing various artistic expressions and reinforcing the cultural memory of the Tibetan people. The epic's continued relevance is evident as it is recognized by UNESCO as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, underscoring its vital role in the cultural narrative of Asia.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Epic of King Gesar (Tibetan: གེ་སར་རྒྱལ་པོ་, Gesar Gyelpo; Mongolian: Гэсэрийн тууль, Geseriyn tuul; also Geser) is the world's longest surviving epic poem — with more than one million verses in its extended versions, far exceeding the combined length of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey — performed and transmitted across Tibet, Mongolia, and adjacent Himalayan and Central Asian cultures over a period of approximately a thousand years (from c. 10th–11th century CE to the present). The epic narrates the life of the divine hero-king Gesar of Ling — a supernatural warrior king sent by the divine realm to conquer the demons and enemies of the dharma, unite the land, and establish a golden age of peace and justice — and encompasses his miraculous birth, his trials and contests for kingship, his thirty-plus military campaigns against demon-kings and human enemies, and his eventual departure from the human world. The epic's core narrative combines Tibetan Buddhist cosmology (Gesar as an emanation of Padmasambhava or Avalokitesvara) with the steppe heroic tradition of the Tibetan and Mongolian worlds.

The Epic of King Gesar is a living oral tradition — performed by specialist bards (grung-mkhan in Tibetan) who claim to receive the epic through visionary experience and dreams rather than deliberate memorisation, a tradition of inspired recitation unique in world epic literature. Gesar bards may perform for days, reciting episodes spontaneously in a state of trance-like inspiration, and different regions have different versions of the epic — the Tibetan, Mongolian, Buriat, Kalmyk, and other versions all have distinctive narrative traditions. The oral tradition is still active: in Tibet, the Gesar bards continue to perform, and the epic has been partially written down in a standardised Tibetan edition running to more than 120 volumes.

The Epic of King Gesar was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009 (jointly by China).
